courseFacts.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
courseFacts.name: Introduction to Data Science
courseFacts.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
courseFacts.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
courseFacts.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Actual R-based cleaning, visualisation, spatial/text data analysis and independent data research support archaeological datasets and interpretation. They do not by themselves supply archaeometric laboratory training.

courseFacts.description2: Introduces Earth Science by focusing on interactions among the deep earth, lithosphere and hydrosphere. Highlights key cycles shaping Earth’s surface and includes indoor/outdoor labs and a multi‑day field excursion.
courseFacts.name: Dynamic Earth
courseFacts.profile: Introduces Earth science by linking surface geology to deep-Earth and geophysical processes. Students study rocks, minerals, sedimentation, deformation, stratigraphy, plate tectonics, seismology, the mantle and core, and interactions with climate and other Earth systems. Field and practical work teaches observation and measurement, rock and mineral identification, and reconstruction of geological history. An Ardennes field investigation produces a geological cross-section, stratigraphic column and interpretive report.
courseFacts.topics: Plate tectonics and the Wilson cycle; Minerals and rock formation; Volcanism and metamorphism; Sedimentation and facies; Structural deformation; Stratigraphy and palaeontology; Seismology and seismic waves; Geomagnetism and gravity; Mantle and core processes; Earth-system and climate interactions; Geological history; Geohazards
courseFacts.methods: Geological field observation and measurement; Rock and mineral identification; Geological mapping and profiling; Stratigraphic-column construction; Geological cross-section construction; Sediment and facies interpretation; Geological-history reconstruction

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Actual rock/mineral identification, field observation, stratigraphy, geological mapping and history reconstruction materially support the landscape and environmental context of archaeological inquiry. Geological fieldwork is not described as archaeological excavation.

courseFacts.description2: Provides hands‑on experience with GIS and data integration using geospatial data from satellites and drones. Uncovers how human actions impact ecosystems and climate and promotes sustainable practices through research projects.
courseFacts.name: Earth Observation
courseFacts.profile: Develops geospatial analysis for investigating environmental change and designing responses to Earth-system problems. Hands-on ArcGIS Pro work covers spatial data models, georeferencing, projections, visualization, queries, transformations and surface analysis. Remote-sensing foundations extend into spectral signatures, acquisition systems, preprocessing and image processing. A collaborative case study applies geospatial methods to an environmental research question.
courseFacts.discipline: Geographic information science; Remote sensing; Environmental science
courseFacts.topics: Spatial concepts and data models; Geospatial databases; Georeferencing and map projections; Spatial visualization; Spatial queries and transformations; Surface analysis; Earth-observation tools; Spectral signatures; Remote-sensing acquisition systems; Image preprocessing and processing; Environmental geospatial applications
courseFacts.methods: ArcGIS Pro spatial analysis; Spatial-data collection and database management; Georeferencing and coordinate transformation; Geospatial visualization and queries; Surface analysis; Remote-sensing preprocessing; Image processing; Geospatial case-study design

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Actual ArcGIS Pro, spatial databases, georeferencing, surface analysis, remote-sensing processing and environmental case research support spatial landscape inquiry. A later accepted schedule must satisfy the formal ENSGATE101 prerequisite and actual offerings.

courseFacts.description2: Explores interactions among biosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and atmosphere. Teaches system modelling, uses proxies and isotope tracers to study past and future climates and includes a field trip focused on greenhouse gas pathways.
courseFacts.name: Earth System Science Tools

ledger.contributionAndLimit: The full description supports system modelling, proxies, isotope tracers and past/future climate inquiry, with a greenhouse-gas field trip. This supports environmental reconstruction within the stated scope; archaeological dating or specialist laboratory competence is not invented. ENSGATE101 is a formal prerequisite.

courseFacts.description2: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.
courseFacts.name: Modern History
courseFacts.profile: Surveys economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present while questioning the meaning and periodization of modernity. Students examine industrialization, political ideologies, nationalism, imperialism, migration, world wars, revolution, decolonization, the Cold War and globalization. Historical research and essays connect specific questions to evidence. A group project analyzes historical visions of the future as products of their own contexts and compares them with subsequent developments.
courseFacts.topics: Modernity and periodization; Industrialization and reform; Political ideologies and nationalism; Migration and imperialism; National, class, gender and racial identities; World wars; Russian Revolution and Soviet history; Democracy and dictatorship; Cold War; Decolonization; Globalization; Historical visions of the future
courseFacts.methods: Historical contextualization; Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Source triangulation; Historical research-question development

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Primary/secondary-source criticism, contextualisation and historical research support understanding the modern formation, colonial legacies and interpretation of heritage. The 1815-to-present remit is not deep-time archaeological coverage.

courseFacts.description2: Examines the rise and fall of empires and the contested concept of empire. Discusses oppressive and benevolent features of empires, covers key theories on empires and power politics and analyses major historical examples.
courseFacts.name: History of Empires
courseFacts.profile: Examines empires comparatively across global history, from ancient Persia, Rome and China to early-modern and modern imperial powers and contemporary claims to imperial status. Students analyze expansion, administration, military and economic systems, legitimacy, ideology, culture, decline and legacies. The course combines theories of empire with historically specific cases, historiographical discussion, source analysis and an independently developed research essay.
courseFacts.topics: Concepts and theories of empire; Imperial rise, expansion and decline; Administration and succession; Military and economic structures; Imperial ideologies and legitimacy; Culture and empire; Ancient and medieval empires; European overseas empires; Modern Asian and Eurasian empires; American power; Contemporary and future empires; Imperial legacies
courseFacts.methods: Comparative historical analysis; Historiographical analysis; Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Historical research-question development

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Actual ancient Persia, Rome and China alongside later empires provide comparative imperial administration, society and power inquiry, with historiography and primary-source research. This adds meaningful ancient-world historical interpretation without claiming excavation methods.

courseFacts.description2: Provides a chronological overview of warfare in the Western world from antiquity to the present. Covers weapons, technology, strategy, defence, mercenaries, cavalry, chivalry, Blitzkrieg, guerrilla warfare and nuclear arsenals, illustrating competition for mastery in Western history.
courseFacts.name: Ways of War
courseFacts.profile: Surveys Western warfare from antiquity to the present and examines the contested claim that a distinctive military trajectory helped produce Western global dominance. Weapons, technology, strategy, tactics, institutions and soldiers' experience are studied across land, sea and air warfare. Research analyzes a strategic text, a commander's performance or a battle from the individual soldier's perspective, using primary sources and historical scholarship.
courseFacts.topics: Western warfare and global power; Ancient infantry and Roman warfare; Medieval warfare; Gunpowder and naval warfare; Overseas conquest; Dynastic and national warfare; Industrialization of war; World wars; Cold War and nuclear strategy; Guerrilla warfare and terrorism; Military leadership; Soldiers' experience, morale and cohesion; Future warfare
courseFacts.methods: Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Historiographical critique of strategic texts; Historical analysis of military command; Soldier-centered battle analysis; Analysis of diaries, memoirs and combat accounts

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Ancient-to-modern warfare, material technologies, institutions and source-based analysis support a bounded study of conflict and past societies. It is a complementary historical contribution, not a generic substitute for archaeology.

courseFacts.description2: This course introduces students to Native American history and life from the 19th through the 21st century.  It argues that power, fear, misogyny, education, genocide, and resilience shape the Indigenous past and present. Topics we explore include the “Stolen Lives” of Indian children forcibly taken from their homes and placed in Indian Boarding Schools from the 1830’s through the 1990’s; Murdered and Missing Indigenous Women and Girls in the twenty-first century; and the individual and community forms of cultural resistance and environmental regeneration that connect past with present and future generations. We learn from the Native American scholars and 2Spirit youth that speak to and with the class. Exchange of cultural and intellectual knowledge also happens when we work with Lakota students to address contemporary challenges. Legislation, memoir, novels, and Indigenous children’s stories are central to our studies. So are the analyses of contemporary music and artistic expressions and exhibitions, as well as Hollywood and Indigenous film featuring Native American histories and lives.
courseFacts.name: Native American Histories
courseFacts.profile: Studies Native American social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present through Indigenous perspectives and collaborative inquiry. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to contemporary resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, relational accountability and reciprocity inform work with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders. Arts-based collaborations and a public-history project develop respectful, accessible accounts of historical and contemporary issues.
courseFacts.discipline: Indigenous studies; Social and cultural history; Public history
courseFacts.topics: Indigenous histories and ways of knowing; Colonialism and white saviourism; Indian wars; Boarding schools and childhood trauma; Institutional confinement; Adoption and blood quantum; Gendered violence and missing Indigenous people; Traditional ecological knowledge; Food sovereignty; Decolonization and Indigenization; Cultural resistance and resurgence; Indigenous storytelling and public history
courseFacts.methods: Indigenous storywork and relational historical inquiry; Primary-source and oral-history analysis; Arts-based collaborative inquiry; Photo/Voice photography and audio narratives; Historical contextualization of contemporary issues; Public-history multimedia production

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Indigenous storywork, relational accountability, oral/primary sources and public-history collaboration support ethical heritage and community inquiry, including dispossession and environmental knowledge. Native American modern histories are not a replacement for world prehistory.

courseFacts.description2: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.
courseFacts.name: Researching the “American Century”

ledger.contributionAndLimit: The full current description supports research-question formulation, source criticism and an interdisciplinary historical paper. No archived Walcheren excavation profile or unstated deep-time content is inherited.

courseFacts.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
courseFacts.name: Introduction to Sociology
courseFacts.profile: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.
courseFacts.topics: Sociological imagination and knowledge; Social structure and socialization; Classical social theory; Colonialism and the formation of sociology; Solidarity and modernity; Identity, belonging and othering; Groups and social networks; Capital, class and mobility; Race and gender inequality; Global inequality and migration; Education and labour-market inequality
courseFacts.methods: Theory-guided sociological case analysis; Comparative analysis of sociological perspectives; Library-based social-science research; Sociological research-question formulation

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Social boundaries, stratification, race/gender/class and library-based theory-guided inquiry support interpretation of social organisation and contemporary heritage publics. Archaeological evidence and ancient social structures still require their own substantive study.

courseFacts.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
courseFacts.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
courseFacts.profile: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
courseFacts.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination
courseFacts.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Interviews, ethnography, participatory/visual and archival inquiry, coding and team research support community heritage and interpretation research. These are actual methods, not a claim of excavation competence.

courseFacts.description2: Provides an introduction to Western art history, tracing major artistic movements from the late Middle Ages to the present. Through close study of key paintings and their makers, students gain insight into evolving styles, techniques and cultural influences.
courseFacts.name: Introduction to Western Art History
courseFacts.profile: Surveys Western art from late-medieval and Renaissance painting to contemporary practice. Students relate artists, styles and movements to social, religious, political and cultural change, with sustained attention to the close examination of paintings. Practical assignments develop analysis of composition, space, form, tone and colour. A term paper studies a painting on location, combining visual interpretation with art-historical evidence and terminology.
courseFacts.topics: Late-medieval and Renaissance art; Mannerism; Baroque and Rococo; Enlightenment and Romanticism; Realism and Impressionism; Post-Impressionism, Symbolism and Art Nouveau; Modernism and Cubism; Interwar art; Postwar and postmodern art; Contemporary art; Artistic form and historical context
courseFacts.methods: Close visual analysis of paintings; Composition, space, form, tone and colour analysis; On-site artwork study; Historical contextualization; Art-historical text analysis

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Close visual analysis, on-site artwork study and historical contextualisation supply methods for interpreting artistic material and its social/religious settings. Its post-medieval Western painting emphasis is bounded rather than equated with world archaeology.

courseFacts.description2: Explores ancient craft production from around the world. Examines how making objects shaped human development and how ancient solutions can inform modern sustainability.
courseFacts.name: Introduction to World Archaeology
courseFacts.profile: Examines how making objects shaped communities and identities from the Neolithic through antiquity across Europe, Asia and Africa. Artefacts, production technologies and craft organization are interpreted in relation to social status, religion, gender, exchange and environmental settings. Students produce an archaeological catalogue description and technical drawings, research a craft-related question and design a hands-on educational game. A small contemporary-archaeology project collects local material evidence and proposes a testable interpretation.
courseFacts.discipline: Archaeology; Material culture studies; Ancient social history
courseFacts.topics: Materiality, craft and cognition; Settlement and landscape; Neolithic and Bronze Age communities; Craft production and social hierarchy; Trade and exchange; Pottery and iconography; Seals, textiles and elite identities; Domestic and urban craft spaces; Archaeological interpretation; Ancient technology and community identity; Contemporary archaeology
courseFacts.methods: Artefact observation, measurement and cataloguing; Archaeological technical drawing; Visual and stylistic analysis; Comparative material-culture analysis; Archaeological database and literature research; Material-evidence-based argumentation; Archaeological educational-game design; Contemporary archaeological data collection and hypothesis development

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Direct material-culture archaeology includes craft production, social identity and exchange across ancient Europe, Asia and Africa, artefact observation/cataloguing, technical drawing, database research and a contemporary material-evidence project. This is strong substantive archaeology, not title-only adjacency.

courseFacts.description2: Examines the artistic, historical and ethical dimensions of African art. Highlights distinct forms and cultural significance, considers influence on Western modernism and addresses looting, colonial-era acquisitions and repatriation efforts.
courseFacts.name: African Art & Heritage
courseFacts.profile: Introduces African art and heritage with particular attention to western African visual traditions and their cultural, religious and social meanings. Students study sculpture, masks and other forms across regional contexts before tracing African art's role in European modernism, the Harlem Renaissance and African artistic renewal. Colonial dispossession, museum collecting and restitution form a major later strand. An independent paper develops a research question supported by scholarly evidence.
courseFacts.discipline: African art history; Cultural heritage studies; Museum studies
courseFacts.topics: Western African artistic traditions; Sculpture, masks and visual languages; Art, religion and social authority; Regional traditions in Nigeria, the Niger region, Atlantic forests and Congo; African influences on European modernism; Harlem Renaissance and diaspora; Art Nègre and the Ecole de Dakar; Colonial looting; Universal museums; Museum acquisition and display; Restitution and repatriation
courseFacts.methods: Visual and contextual art-historical analysis; Comparative interpretation of artistic traditions; Analysis of primary artistic and critical texts; Heritage-restitution case analysis; Scholarly literature review and annotated bibliography; Independent art-historical research

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Regional African artistic material, cultural/religious meaning, museum collection, colonial dispossession and restitution offer direct heritage and material-culture content, with independent research.

courseFacts.description2: This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.
courseFacts.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean

ledger.contributionAndLimit: The full description supports Renaissance painting, sculpture and architecture in Mediterranean/global trade, colonisation and exchange. It adds specific cross-cultural material interpretation without invented archaeological field methods.

courseFacts.description2: The invention of democracy in classical Greece changed the nature of community decision-making, perhaps forever. This process is reflected in the material culture of the period. By examining the archaeology of community & democracy in early-democratic Greece, this course goes in search of ancient lessons for the modern world.
courseFacts.name: Greek Archaeology

ledger.contributionAndLimit: The full description explicitly studies archaeology and material culture of community and democracy in early-democratic Greece. Give this direct archaeological contribution full weight despite absent outline fields; do not invent a technical excavation syllabus.

courseFacts.description2: Examines debates on modern art through various themes. Focuses on the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions, exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies.
courseFacts.name: Modern Art & Modern Museums
courseFacts.profile: Examines modern and contemporary art from the late nineteenth century to the present together with the institutions that shape its display and reception. Students study avant-gardes, abstraction, modernist design, figuration, postmodern and conceptual practices, and global contemporary art. Museums, exhibitions, curatorial choices and Eurocentric narratives are treated critically. An independently researched paper develops a focused art-historical question, methods and evidence-based argument.
courseFacts.topics: Modernism and avant-gardes; Cubism and abstraction; Modern architecture and design; Figuration and Mexican muralism; Abstract Expressionism; Minimalism and Pop Art; Postmodernism and conceptual art; Photography, installation, performance and video art; Globalization and contemporary art; Authorship, originality and medium; Museums, curating and reception; Eurocentrism in art history
courseFacts.methods: Art-historical interpretation and contextual analysis; Critical analysis of museums and curatorial practices; Scholarly literature review; Independent art-historical research

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Actual museums, curating, display, reception and Eurocentric narratives, with independent art-historical research, directly support heritage interpretation. Its modern-art emphasis is distinct from prehistoric regional content.

courseFacts.description2:
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century._x000D_
Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants._x000D_
This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.
courseFacts.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
courseFacts.profile: Studies Athenian democracy through history, archaeology, literature, art and religion, including its exclusions and moments of crisis. Students analyze citizenship, social divisions, myth, ritual and cultural expression through primary texts and material evidence. A historically grounded assembly simulation explores political decision-making. Research reports connect ancient democracy to the present, while a collective cultural project for Middelburg experiments with participatory democratic collaboration.
courseFacts.discipline: Ancient history; Archaeology; Classical studies; Political sociology
courseFacts.topics: Development of Athenian democracy; Citizenship and property classes; Women, foreigners and excluded groups; Democratic reform and participation; Labour and community; Myth, religion and civic identity; Tragedy and satire; Demagoguery, tyranny and democratic resilience; Assembly debate and voting; Ancient and modern democracy; Cultural expression and community
courseFacts.methods: Primary-text and archaeological-evidence analysis; Historical character research; CREATE reading method; Historically grounded assembly simulation; Ancient-modern comparative analysis; Participatory cultural-project design

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Primary texts and archaeological material, ancient Athenian social divisions, civic/religious culture, a grounded assembly simulation and participatory cultural project support ancient heritage, interpretation and public life.

courseFacts.description2: Explores media technologies before digital culture. Studies cassette tapes, typewriters and early printing as material objects that carry meaning; includes hands‑on experiments; no technical background required.
courseFacts.name: Media Archaeology
courseFacts.profile: Examines media technologies as material and cultural artifacts, moving from early print through optical projection, telegraphy, typewriters and analogue sound to digital networks. Students apply recurring theoretical perspectives to how physical properties and infrastructures shape communication, knowledge and memory. Hands-on object, listening and recording exercises connect historical evidence to lived experience. Independent research analyzes a selected media object or phenomenon using appropriate media-archaeological methods.
courseFacts.discipline: Media archaeology; Media history; Material culture studies
courseFacts.topics: Media materiality and memory; Print culture; Optics and projection; Telegraphy and infrastructure; Mechanical inscription; Broadcasting and sound fidelity; Portable analogue media; Cassette revival; Computing and networks; Media geology; Technological obsolescence; Mechanical reproduction and aura
courseFacts.methods: Media-archaeological artifact analysis; Historical and technical media comparison; Facsimile and manuscript-print analysis; Media-protocol investigation; Comparative listening and sound-fidelity analysis; Analogue recording exercises; Historical media-object research

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Actual material analysis of print, optical, mechanical and analogue media, hands-on object/recording exercises and historical media-object research support a specific material-heritage and communication direction. The media-archaeology label is not taken as excavation training.

courseFacts.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
courseFacts.name: Personal & Professional Development
courseFacts.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
courseFacts.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
courseFacts.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Mandatory academic development, research literacy and community engagement; no excavation counterpart.

courseFacts.description2: Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses.
courseFacts.name: Sustainability Essentials I
courseFacts.profile: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.
courseFacts.discipline: Sustainability science; Applied mathematics; Chemistry; Physics
courseFacts.topics: Planetary boundaries and the Anthropocene; Exponential growth and environmental change; Graphs, rates and uncertainty; Dynamic systems; Chemical bonds, reactions and equilibria; Ocean acidification and nutrient cycles; Thermodynamics and entropy; Greenhouse gases and energy; Ozone depletion; Newtonian mechanics, stress and strain; Biopolymers and material properties
courseFacts.methods: Graph interpretation and comparison; Fermi estimation; Difference-equation and first-order linear differential-equation modelling; Elementary differentiation and integration; Biopolymer preparation; Strength and elasticity measurement; Iterative experimental improvement

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Actual scientific,chemical/mechanical and material-experiment foundations support landscape/material inquiry and formal EarthObservation/Tools preparation.

courseFacts.description2: Builds on Sustainability Essentials I. Applies tools and knowledge to a real‑world sustainability case study and allows students to delve deeper into aspects connected to their field of interest.
courseFacts.name: Sustainability Essentials II
courseFacts.profile: Connects wave physics, chemistry and materials science to sustainability questions. Students study wave behaviour and observation methods, chemical analysis, microscopic material structure and macroscopic stress and strain. Practical sessions include wave applications and chemistry laboratory work. Reflective inquiries and a final project critically assess sustainability campaigns, identify greenwashing and communicate evidence-based improvements to a public audience.
courseFacts.discipline: Physics; Chemistry; Materials science; Sustainability studies
courseFacts.topics: Electromagnetic and mechanical waves; Wave composition and interference; Optical spectroscopy; Electron microscopy; Inorganic and organic chemistry; Chemical testing; Material structure and crystallography; Stress and strain; Sustainable material design; Geological wave applications; Nuclear power and waste; Greenwashing
courseFacts.methods: Oscilloscope wave visualization; Optical-spectroscopy interpretation; Fourier wave analysis; Copper dissolution and chemical analysis; Laboratory logbook documentation; Stress-strain analysis; Mohr's-circle application; Evidence-based greenwashing case analysis; Public sustainability-communication design

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Actual wave,spectroscopy,material-structure and chemical experiments support physical material/context methods; no invented archaeometry or excavation sequence.

courseFacts.description2: Explores soils and aquifers through fieldwork and lab analyses. Covers soil formation, properties, health and remediation and investigates mapping aquifers for geothermal energy, coastal defence and freshwater resource assessment.
courseFacts.name: Soils & Aquifers
courseFacts.profile: Examines soils and shallow aquifers through soil science, environmental chemistry and applied geophysics. Soil formation, functions, quality and threats connect to texture, structure, composition, biological activity and salinization. Field sampling and laboratory investigations characterize soil properties and sediment-cell behaviour. Seismic, electrical-resistivity and electromagnetic surveys investigate physical and geophysical properties of soils and aquifers. Students document procedures and observations, process field data in Excel, interpret results and develop evidence-based field and laboratory reports.
courseFacts.discipline: Soil science; Hydrogeology; Applied geophysics; Environmental chemistry
courseFacts.topics: Soil formation, functions and taxonomy; Soil quality, amendments and threats; Soil texture, structure and aggregate stability; Soil moisture and organic matter; Soil chemistry, pH and metals; Soil biology; Sediment-cell behaviour; Shallow aquifers, salinization and freshwater interventions; Physical and geophysical properties of soils and aquifers; Seismology; Electrical resistivity; Electromagnetic surveying
courseFacts.methods: Soil coring and field sampling; Visual soil-structure assessment (grass-VESS); Aggregate-stability, texture and sieve tests; Soil pH, moisture, organic-content and leaching analyses; Microscopy and SEM-EDS; Sample preparation for ICP/IC and interpretation of ICP results; Methylene-blue testing with spectrophotometry/titration; Seismic surveying; Electrical-resistivity and electromagnetic surveying; Field-data processing in Excel

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Actual soil,coring,seismic/resistivity/electromagnetic field measurements support landscape/site context. These geological surveys are not archaeological context excavation.

courseFacts.description2: Investigates natural waters and their interactions with rocks, soils and minerals. Examines biogeochemical processes and cycles, including weathering, mineral formation, absorption, water treatment and resource recovery; utilises geochemical modelling and a case study.
courseFacts.name: Environmental Biogeochemistry
courseFacts.profile: Examines chemical and biological controls on near-surface Earth systems, especially interactions among water, minerals, rocks and soils. Students study aqueous composition, equilibrium, speciation, carbonate and redox chemistry, adsorption, weathering and biomineralization. Laboratory investigations and geochemical modelling connect these processes to contaminant behaviour, wastewater treatment, remediation and resource recovery. A project applies geochemical principles to a current environmental issue.
courseFacts.topics: Natural-water composition; Chemical equilibrium and ionic activity; Aqueous speciation and complexation; Mineral saturation, precipitation and dissolution; Carbonate equilibria, alkalinity and buffering; Ocean acidification; Redox processes and microbial controls; Adsorption and mineral surfaces; Weathering and clay formation; Biomineralization; Contaminant transport; Environmental remediation and resource recovery
courseFacts.methods: Geochemical equilibrium and speciation modelling; Geochemist's Workbench; Piper diagrams; Pourbaix and stability diagrams; Laboratory geochemical investigations; Geochemical data interpretation

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Actual mineral/water/soil chemistry, equilibrium/speciation/redox and geochemical modelling/laboratory investigations support preservation/environmental material context; no claimed archaeological dating curriculum.

courseFacts.description2: Provides in‑depth geoscience research into resource and environmental challenges such as nuclear waste storage, geothermal energy and CO₂ capture. Students conduct literature reviews and produce class reports for presentation to a professional conference.
courseFacts.name: Earth's Resources

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Description-only geoscience resource/environmental research,literature reports and conference presentation support landscape research at stated scope. No unprovided excavation outline.

courseFacts.description2: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.
courseFacts.name: R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation
courseFacts.profile: Studies resource circularity through solar-panel recycling, metal recovery from electronic waste, and soil remediation using plants and mycelium. Theory and extensive laboratory work connect material composition and separation technologies to resource yields, environmental consequences and recycling constraints. Students develop leaching protocols, analyze metal concentrations and recovery, cultivate fungal networks, and use microscopy to characterize materials and mycelium growth.
courseFacts.discipline: Environmental chemistry; Materials recycling; Environmental biotechnology
courseFacts.topics: Circular resource supply; Solar-cell and solar-panel recycling; Delamination and material separation; Electronic waste; Pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy; Precious-metal recovery; Plastic-recycling legislation; Phytoremediation; Mycoremediation; Mycelium-based soil amendments
courseFacts.methods: Solar-panel dismantling and physical separation; Chemical leaching; Experimental-protocol design; ICP metal analysis; Electrochemical recovery; Scanning electron microscopy and EDS; Mycelium cultivation and growth characterization; Recovery-yield and resource-potential calculations

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Actual material separation,SEM/EDS,electrochemical recovery and protocol development provide complementary scientific material methods; modern waste/recovery is not archaeological artefact typology.

courseFacts.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
courseFacts.name: Mathematical Methods
courseFacts.profile: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
courseFacts.topics: Functions and limits; Continuity; Differentiation; Optimization; Taylor series; Complex numbers; Definite and indefinite integrals; Integration techniques; First-order differential equations; Population-growth and predator–prey models; Second-order linear differential equations; Dynamic models
courseFacts.methods: Analytical differentiation and integration; Taylor approximation; Newton's method; Numerical integration; Euler's method; Analytical solution of differential equations; Computer algebra with Mathematica; Dynamic-model implementation and analysis

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Calculus,differential equations and actual dynamic modelling support environmental reconstruction and preparation for rigorous statistics; no archaeology dataset promised.

courseFacts.description2: Introduces systems of equations, vectors, matrices and linear spaces with emphasis on visual and conceptual understanding. Applies concepts across fields and includes hands‑on exercises using computer algebra software.
courseFacts.name: Linear Algebra
courseFacts.profile: Develops linear algebra from systems of equations and matrix operations to vector spaces, linear transformations, eigenvalues and orthogonality. Students study least-squares approximation, symmetric matrices, quadratic forms and singular value decomposition. Applications include discrete signals, difference equations, Markov chains, dynamical systems, graphics and principal component analysis. Mathematica exercises teach computer-algebra approaches to larger problems alongside analytical problem-solving.
courseFacts.topics: Linear systems and matrix algebra; Linear independence, span, basis, dimension and rank; Linear transformations; Determinants and invertibility; Vector spaces; Eigenvalues and eigenvectors; Difference equations and Markov chains; Discrete signals and Fourier series; Orthogonality and inner products; Quadratic forms and constrained optimization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis
courseFacts.methods: Row reduction; Matrix factorization and diagonalization; Change of basis; Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization; Orthogonal projection; Least-squares fitting and QR factorization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis; Mathematica computer-algebra computation

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Linear algebra,least-squares,SVD and spatial/dynamic representations support quantitative/spatial interpretation.

courseFacts.description2: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
courseFacts.name: Probability & Statistics
courseFacts.profile: Provides a rigorous introduction to probability and mathematical statistics, from probability spaces and random variables to multivariate distributions and statistical inference. Students study estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and maximum-likelihood methods, followed by an introduction to Bayesian reasoning. Mathematica simulations verify analytical results. A substantial project implements and compares random-sampling algorithms, including inverse sampling, accept-reject sampling and Gibbs sampling.
courseFacts.topics: Probability spaces and conditional probability; Random variables and expectation; Moment-generating functions; Discrete and continuous distributions; Multivariate and conditional distributions; Transformations and correlation; Sampling and order statistics; Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests; Estimation efficiency; Bayesian inference; Monte Carlo methods
courseFacts.methods: Analytical probability calculation; Maximum-likelihood estimation and testing; Chi-square tests; Bootstrap; EM algorithm; Bayesian updating; Inverse-transform sampling; Accept-reject sampling; Gibbs sampling; Monte Carlo simulation in Mathematica

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Rigorous probability,inference,estimation and MonteCarlo sampling support archaeological data uncertainty and evidence analysis; no archaeometric lab equivalence.

courseFacts.description2: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.
courseFacts.name: Writing Art's Histories

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Actual art-historiography,interpretation,authorship andidentity methods support critical material/heritage interpretation. Description-only, no invented new syllabus.

courseFacts.description2: Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links between past and present.
courseFacts.name: Media & Race
courseFacts.profile: Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture. Theatre, photographs, news, film, music, tourism and literature reveal both oppression and resistance. Students investigate exclusion, racialized bodies, youth, marginalized storytelling and imagined futures. Participant observation, archival research, a documentary podcast and a cross-cultural Photo/Voice project connect historical analysis with lived experience and representation.
courseFacts.discipline: Cultural history; Media studies; Race and ethnicity studies; American studies
courseFacts.topics: Racial construction and whiteness; Media, power and representation; Leisure, tourism and racial identity; Crime, punishment and the racialized body; Asian-American exclusion; Japanese-American incarceration; Childhood and youth; Marginalized and Indigenous storytelling; Racial extremism and propaganda; Alienation and community; Food, environment and cultural nourishment; Afrofuturism and Indigenous futurisms
courseFacts.methods: Participant observation; Archival primary-source research; Historical media analysis; Documentary podcast research, scripting and audio production; Photo/Voice photography and audio narrative; Cross-cultural interpretive reflection

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Actual colonial/racial culturalrepresentation,archival/observational evidence and publicmedia work support heritage exclusion/restitution interpretation; American focus remains distinct from worldprehistory.

courseFacts.description2: Introduces development of the documentary form. Students write a theoretical paper and produce a short documentary film, fostering understanding of documentary diversity and providing analytical tools for documentary study.
courseFacts.name: The Documentary
courseFacts.profile: Studies documentary history, modes and styles alongside practical documentary production. Students analyze nonfiction representation in historical, social, ethical and aesthetic contexts, from early and Soviet filmmaking through direct cinema and contemporary forms. Topics include propaganda, advocacy, ethnography, history, nature, audio and interactive documentary. Production workshops guide a short film through preproduction, filming and postproduction, with reflection on interviewing and representational choices.
courseFacts.discipline: Documentary studies; Film studies; Media production
courseFacts.topics: Documentary definition, modes and ethics; Early documentary and city symphonies; Soviet filmmaking; European documentary traditions; Direct cinema and cinéma vérité; Audio and public-affairs documentary; Propaganda and advocacy; Historical and ethnographic documentary; Nature documentary; Mockumentary; Interactive and autobiographical documentary; Documentary aesthetics
courseFacts.methods: Critical documentary analysis; Historical and contextual film comparison; Documentary research and interviewing; Script, storyboard and shot-list development; Preproduction planning; Documentary filming and postproduction; Reflective evaluation of production practice

ledger.contributionAndLimit: Actual documentaryhistory,ethics,representation,interviewing andproduction support public communication of pasts, not an excavation internship.
